wizard.title: How to play {game}
wizard.wiezen.1.title: The goal
wizard.wiezen.1.body: Four players, each on their own. Every deal you get 13 cards. First you promise how many tricks you will take (that is the bidding), then you try to make good on it. Make your promise and you win points from the others.
wizard.wiezen.2.title: Cards and trump
wizard.wiezen.2.body: Ace is the highest card, then king, queen, jack, ten … down to the two. The last card dealt is turned face up: that suit is trump. A trump card always beats a plain card.
wizard.wiezen.3.title: Bidding
wizard.wiezen.3.body: You choose what you promise. 'Ask & join' means: I want a partner and together we take 8 tricks. If nobody joins you may play alone (5 tricks). Stronger hands bid higher: abondance (9 or more tricks alone) or misère (not a single trick). Hold exactly three aces and you must call troel: the player with the fourth ace becomes your partner, leads that ace, and its suit is trump.
wizard.wiezen.4.title: Playing tricks
wizard.wiezen.4.body: The leader plays a card; the others follow clockwise. You must follow suit if you can. If you cannot, you are free to trump or throw something away. The highest trump wins the trick, otherwise the highest card of the suit led. The winner leads the next trick.
wizard.wiezen.5.title: Scoring
wizard.wiezen.5.body: Make your contract and the opponents pay you; miss it and you pay them. Every trick above your target earns extra, every trick short costs you. The app does all the maths — you get a summary after each deal.
wizard.manille.1.title: The goal
wizard.manille.1.body: Manille is played in two fixed teams: you and the player opposite you are partners. Together you collect card points. Take more than half and your team wins the deal.
wizard.manille.2.title: The ten rules
wizard.manille.2.body: Careful: here the ten (the 'manille') is the highest card, above the ace. The order is 10, ace, king, queen, jack, 9, 8, 7. The ten is worth 5 points, the ace 4, the king 3, the queen 2 and the jack 1 — 60 points in total.
wizard.manille.3.title: Trump and the duty to trump
wizard.manille.3.body: The dealer picks the trump suit. You must follow suit. If you cannot, you must trump — and if you can overtrump, you must. Only when you have no trump left may you discard.
wizard.manille.4.title: Scoring
wizard.manille.4.body: After eight tricks you count each team's card points. The team above 30 wins the deal and scores the difference with 30. At 30-30 nobody scores. First team to 101 points wins the session.
wizard.bieden.1.title: The goal
wizard.bieden.1.body: Bieden is played in two fixed teams. You promise a number of points (at least 100) and try to collect them with your partner. There are 151 points in play.
wizard.bieden.2.title: Card values
wizard.bieden.2.body: In the trump suit the jack is the highest card (20 points), then the nine (14), ace (11), ten (10), king (3) and queen (2). In the other suits the ace leads (11), then ten (10), king (3), queen (2), jack (1). The last trick is worth 10 extra points.
wizard.bieden.3.title: Bidding and trump
wizard.bieden.3.body: Each player gets one chance to bid or pass; raises go in steps of ten. The highest bidder leads — and the suit of that first card immediately becomes trump. What makes this game special: you may always trump, even when you could follow suit.
wizard.bieden.4.title: Scoring
wizard.bieden.4.body: If your team collects at least the points you bid, you score that bid. If you fall short, the amount goes to the opponents instead. First team to 500 points wins.
coach.tip.troel: Someone holds three aces, so troel is compulsory. The player with the fourth ace is automatically the partner and leads — that first card sets the trump.
coach.tip.joinYes: Your hand is strong enough to join: together you need 8 tricks.
coach.tip.joinNo: Joining is risky with this hand — 8 tricks together is a lot to ask. Passing is always allowed.
coach.tip.askStrong: Strong hand ({hp} honour points, {trumps} trumps). Asking is worth considering: you look for a partner for 8 tricks together.
coach.tip.askWeak: Weak hand ({hp} honour points). Passing is usually wisest — waiting costs you nothing.
coach.tip.alone: Nobody joined. Playing alone means taking 5 tricks on your own. In doubt? Better to pass.
coach.tip.chooseTrump: Pick the suit where you hold the most and the highest cards — that becomes your trump.
coach.tip.lead: You lead. A high card in your longest suit is usually a safe start.
coach.tip.leadSetsTrump: You lead and your first card sets the trump. So pick the suit you are strongest in.
coach.tip.mustFollow: You must follow suit — only those cards are clickable now.
coach.tip.cannotFollow: You do not hold the suit led. You are free to choose: trump to take the trick, or discard a card you do not need.
coach.tip.manilleTrump: You deal and pick the trump. Take the suit you hold most of — ideally with the ten or the ace in it.
coach.tip.manilleLead: You lead. Remember: the ten is the highest card here and worth 5 points.
coach.tip.manilleMustTrump: You cannot follow suit, so you must trump (and overtrump if you can).
coach.tip.biedenBidYes: Strong hand ({hp} honour points). A bid of 100 or more is defensible — remember your partner collects points too.
coach.tip.biedenBidNo: Rather weak hand ({hp} honour points). Passing costs nothing; let the opponents take the risk.
coach.tip.biedenLeadSetsTrump: You bid highest, so you lead — and that first card sets the trump.
coach.tip.biedenFollowOrTrump: In bieden you may always trump, even when you could follow suit. Pick whatever pays best.

guide.title: Rules & explanation
guide.intro: Pick a topic. Every chapter walks you through the rules step by step — you can always go back.
guide.readMore: All the rules of this game
guide.basis.title: The basics
guide.basis.summary: What every game in this app has in common: the table, the cards and the trick.
guide.basis.tafel.title: Four players around a table
guide.basis.tafel.body: Every game here is played by four. You sit across from one player and next to two others. Dealing, bidding and playing all go clockwise. The dealer moves on each round, so everyone gets an equal turn at leading.
guide.basis.kaarten.title: The cards
guide.basis.kaarten.body: Wiezen uses the full 52-card pack: everyone gets 13. Manillen and bieden use a short 32-card pack (twos through sixes are removed): everyone gets 8. The ace is usually the highest card, then king (K), queen (Q), jack (J), ten, nine … down to the two.
guide.basis.slag.title: Winning a trick
guide.basis.slag.body: One player leads: they put down a card. The other three then play one card each, clockwise. Those four cards together are a trick. You must follow the suit that was led as long as you still hold it. The highest card in that suit wins — unless someone trumps. Whoever wins the trick leads the next one.
guide.basis.troef.title: What trumps do
guide.basis.troef.body: One suit is trump for the round. Any trump beats any card of another suit, however high: the two of trumps beats the ace of another suit. If several trumps land in one trick, the highest trump wins. How the trump suit gets decided differs per game — that is exactly what separates plain wiezen from kleurenwiezen.
guide.gewoon-wiezen.title: Plain wiezen
guide.gewoon-wiezen.summary: The classic form: the turned last card sets the trump suit.
guide.gewoon-wiezen.troef.title: The trump is face up
guide.gewoon-wiezen.troef.body: After dealing, the last card — the dealer's — is turned face up on the table. That suit is trump for the round. So everyone knows the trump suit before any bidding happens, and you can see at once how many trumps you hold yourself. That is the main information your bid rests on.
guide.gewoon-wiezen.bieden.title: The bidding round
guide.gewoon-wiezen.bieden.body: Bidding starts left of the dealer and goes clockwise. You say what you promise to take, or you pass. Any new bid must sit higher on the ladder than the bid already on the table. Once you have passed you are out. If everybody passes, the cards go back in and the next player deals again — no score.
guide.gewoon-wiezen.vraag.title: Ask & join
guide.gewoon-wiezen.vraag.body: The lowest and most common contract. You say 'I ask': I am looking for a partner. A player after you can 'join'. Together you then need at least 8 of the 13 tricks. Manage it and you both collect points from both opponents; every trick above 8 pays extra. Take 7 or fewer and you pay instead.
guide.gewoon-wiezen.alleen.title: Going alone
guide.gewoon-wiezen.alleen.body: If nobody joins, you face a choice: pass after all, or play alone. Alone means you against three, and you need at least 5 tricks. It pays more than ask & join, but you get no help. Fail and you pay all three opponents.
guide.gewoon-wiezen.troel.title: Troel
guide.gewoon-wiezen.troel.body: Hold exactly three aces and you must call 'troel' — it is not a choice. The player with the fourth ace automatically becomes your partner, even though they do not know it yet. They lead, and they are meant to lead that very ace: its suit becomes trump. Lead anything else and that card's suit becomes trump instead, but you need one more trick — 9 rather than 8. If the caller holds all four aces, the king of hearts holder is the partner and the same rule applies to that king. Troel counts double: both the win and the loss weigh more than an ordinary ask.
guide.gewoon-wiezen.hoog.title: The high contracts
guide.gewoon-wiezen.hoog.body: When you are very strong — or very weak — you bid higher. Abondance: you play alone, choose the trump suit yourself and promise 9, 10, 11 or 12 tricks. Misère: you promise to take no trick at all — one trick and you are out. Open misère is the same, with your cards face up. Solo (all 13 with trumps) and soloslim (all 13 without) sit at the top.
guide.gewoon-wiezen.punten.title: Scoring
guide.gewoon-wiezen.punten.body: Every contract has a fixed value: ask & join 2, alone 3, troel 4, abondance 6 to 9, misère 7, open misère 14, solo 20, soloslim 30. Make your contract and you collect that from each opponent; miss it and you pay the same. For ask, alone and troel the tricks above or below your target count too. It all sums to zero: what one wins, the others lose.
guide.kleurenwiezen.title: Kleurenwiezen
guide.kleurenwiezen.summary: Same rules, but whoever asks names the trump suit themselves.
guide.kleurenwiezen.verschil.title: The only difference
guide.kleurenwiezen.verschil.body: Kleurenwiezen is plain wiezen with one difference: no card is turned up. So the trump suit is not fixed when bidding starts. Every other rule — the ladder, the scores, troel, misère, abondance, following suit — is identical. If you know plain wiezen, you know this too.
guide.kleurenwiezen.vragen.title: Asking in a suit
guide.kleurenwiezen.vragen.body: Whoever asks says which suit in the same breath: 'I ask in hearts'. That suit is trump for the whole round. So you choose yourself — and naturally you choose the suit you are strongest in. If nobody joins and you play alone, your announced suit stays trump; you cannot switch any more.
guide.kleurenwiezen.meegaan.title: What that means for joining
guide.kleurenwiezen.meegaan.body: In plain wiezen you know the trump suit before bidding. Here you hear it only when someone asks — and that instantly tells you something about their hand: they are strong in that suit. So reassess your own hand the moment the suit is named. Three high cards in that suit make joining attractive; none at all and passing is the obvious call. Higher contracts are unchanged: an abondance player still picks their suit after the bidding.
guide.manillen.title: Manillen
guide.manillen.summary: Fixed teams, 32 cards, and the ten is the highest card.
guide.manillen.ploegen.title: Fixed teams
guide.manillen.ploegen.body: Unlike wiezen the partners do not change: you and the player across from you are one team for the whole match. You play with 32 cards, 8 each. You collect card points rather than tricks — what is inside the tricks is what counts.
guide.manillen.rangorde.title: The ten rules
guide.manillen.rangorde.body: Here is the surprise: the ten — the 'manille' — is the highest card, above the ace. The order is 10, A, K, Q, J, 9, 8, 7. Only those top five score: ten 5, ace 4, king 3, queen 2, jack 1. Nine, eight and seven are worth nothing but can still win a trick.
guide.manillen.troefplicht.title: Follow and trump
guide.manillen.troefplicht.body: The dealer picks the trump suit. You must follow the suit led, just as in wiezen. But if you cannot, here you must trump — and if a trump is already down, you must overtrump when you can. Only a player with no trumps left may discard. That sharpens the game: you cannot hoard your trumps.
guide.manillen.punten.title: Scoring
guide.manillen.punten.body: There are 60 points in the pack. After the eight tricks each team counts its card points. The team over 30 wins the round and writes down the difference from 30: take 38 and you score 8. At 30-30 nobody scores. The first team to 101 points wins the match.
guide.bieden.title: Bieden
guide.bieden.summary: A team game where you promise points — and the trump falls with the first card.
guide.bieden.ploegen.title: Teams and target
guide.bieden.ploegen.body: Here too you and the player opposite form a fixed team, with 32 cards and 8 each. You promise points rather than tricks: at least 100 of the 151 in the pack. Reach them with your partner and you write down your bid; fall short and the amount goes to the opposition.
guide.bieden.waarden.title: Card values
guide.bieden.waarden.body: Values depend on the suit. In trumps the jack is by far the highest card (20 points), then the nine (14), the ace (11), the ten (10), the king (3) and the queen (2). In the other suits the usual order holds: ace 11, ten 10, king 3, queen 2, jack 1. The last trick of the round is worth 10 extra — 151 in total.
guide.bieden.veiling.title: The auction and the trump
guide.bieden.veiling.body: Every player gets one chance: bid or pass. Bids go up in tens, starting at 100. The highest bidder leads — and the suit of that very first card becomes trump. So you commit to your trump with your opening move, in full view of everyone.
guide.bieden.punten.title: Free trumping and scoring
guide.bieden.punten.body: The quirk of bieden: you may always trump, even when you could still follow suit. That makes every trick unpredictable. At the end each team counts its points; if the bidding team reaches its bid it writes that bid down, otherwise the opposition gets it. First team to 500 wins.
guide.scorebord.title: The scoreboard
guide.scorebord.summary: For when you are at the table with real cards and only want the score kept.
guide.scorebord.waarvoor.title: What it is for
guide.scorebord.waarvoor.body: The scoreboard plays nothing: it counts. You are at the table with friends and a real pack of cards, and the app keeps the score. You enter two to four names, optionally a target score, and add the points after every round. The standings survive closing the app.
guide.scorebord.manueel.title: Manual mode
guide.scorebord.manueel.body: In manual mode you simply type the points each player took that round — for any game at all. Handy for a game the app does not know, or when you use your own scoring. You can delete a round if you slip up, and choose whether the highest or the lowest score wins.
guide.scorebord.auto.title: Wiezen automatically
guide.scorebord.auto.body: Playing wiezen? Pick the auto mode: you indicate which contract was played (troel included), who played it, who their partner was — or that they went alone — and how many tricks were taken. The app works out the points for all four players with the same rules as the game itself, overtricks and undertricks included. No more arguments at the table.

tile.klaverjassen: Dutch team game with roem melds.
klaverjas.intro: Two fixed teams, 32 cards. Pick the trump suit and score more than the opposition — combinations landing in one trick pay extra roem.
klaverjas.chooseOrPass: Pick a trump suit, or pass.
klaverjas.mustChoose: Everyone passed — you deal, so you must choose.
klaverjas.goal: Target: more points than the opposition (162 + roem to share).
klaverjas.nat: {team} went wet — everything goes to the opposition
wizard.klaverjassen.1.title: The goal
wizard.klaverjassen.1.body: Klaverjassen is played by two fixed teams: you and the player across from you. Each round you get 8 cards from a 32-card pack. One player picks the trump suit; that team then has to score more points than the opposition.
wizard.klaverjassen.2.title: The jack rules
wizard.klaverjassen.2.body: In trumps the jack is the highest card (20 points), then the nine (14), then ace (11), ten (10), king (4) and queen (3). In the other suits the usual order holds: ace 11, ten 10, king 4, queen 3, jack 2. That is 152 points, plus 10 for the last trick.
wizard.klaverjassen.3.title: Choosing trumps
wizard.klaverjassen.3.body: The player left of the dealer gets first refusal, or passes. If everybody passes, the dealer must pick a suit — playing is compulsory. Whoever picks plays for the win together with their partner.
wizard.klaverjassen.4.title: Follow, trump, overtrump
wizard.klaverjassen.4.body: You must follow the suit led. If you cannot, you must trump — and if a trump is already down, you must beat it when you can. If you cannot overtrump it depends on the counting style: Rotterdam makes you play a trump anyway, Amsterdam lets you discard.
wizard.klaverjassen.5.title: Roem and scoring
wizard.klaverjassen.5.body: Three cards in sequence in one suit landing in the same trick is 20 roem; four in sequence 50; four of a kind 100 (four jacks 200). King and queen of trumps from one player is called stuk: 20. If the choosing team falls short they go "wet" and all the points go to the opposition.
guide.klaverjassen.title: Klaverjassen
guide.klaverjassen.summary: The Dutch team game: choose trumps, overtrump, and count roem.
guide.klaverjassen.ploegen.title: Fixed teams
guide.klaverjassen.ploegen.body: You and the player opposite form one team for the whole match. You play with 32 cards, 8 each, so every round is eight tricks. A classic match is a "boompje" of 16 rounds.
guide.klaverjassen.waarden.title: The jack rules
guide.klaverjassen.waarden.body: In trumps the jack counts 20 and the nine 14 — those two together already beat all four aces. Then come ace 11, ten 10, king 4 and queen 3. In the other suits the usual order holds with ace 11, ten 10, king 4, queen 3 and jack 2. That is 152 points in all, and the last trick pays 10 more: 162 per round.
guide.klaverjassen.troef.title: Who picks the trump suit
guide.klaverjassen.troef.body: The player left of the dealer gets first refusal: choose or pass. On a pass it moves clockwise. If everyone passes the dealer must choose — so a round is always played. Whoever chooses takes on, with their partner, the duty to win.
guide.klaverjassen.troefplicht.title: Following, trumping and overtrumping
guide.klaverjassen.troefplicht.body: Following suit is compulsory. If you cannot follow you must trump; if a trump is already down and you hold a higher one, you must beat it. If you cannot overtrump it differs by region: Rotterdam makes you undertrump, Amsterdam lets you discard — and there, if your partner already holds the trick, you need not trump at all. You pick the counting style at the start.
guide.klaverjassen.roem.title: Roem
guide.klaverjassen.roem.body: Roem are extra points for combinations that land in one and the same trick. Three cards in sequence in one suit: 20. Four in sequence: 50. Four of a kind: 100, and four jacks even 200. If one player puts down both the king and queen of trumps in the same trick that is called stuk and pays 20. The roem goes to the team that wins the trick — even if the opponent played the cards.
guide.klaverjassen.punten.title: Made, wet or pit
guide.klaverjassen.punten.body: After eight tricks each team counts its card points plus roem. The choosing team is "in" as soon as it holds more than the opposition; then each team keeps its own points. Fall short and they are "wet": everything — their own points and the opponents’ — goes to the other team and they get nothing. Win all eight tricks and that is pit, worth 100 on top.
coach.tip.kjChoose: Pick the suit you are strongest in — the trump jack and nine are worth 34 points between them. Weak hand? Better to pass and let someone else carry the risk.
coach.tip.kjMustChoose: Everyone passed, so you must choose. Take the suit you hold the most and the highest of.
coach.tip.kjLead: You lead. The trump jack pulls the trumps out straight away; otherwise an ace in a long suit is a safe start.
coach.tip.kjMustTrump: You cannot follow suit, so you must trump — and overtrump if you can.
tile.belote: The French team game, with annonces.
belote.intro: Two fixed teams, 32 cards. Trumps are offered by a turned-up card; combinations in your hand pay annonces.
belote.nameSuit: Nobody took it. Name another suit, or pass.
belote.redeal: Nobody took trumps — the next dealer deals again.
belote.goal: Target: more points than the opposition (162 + annonces).
belote.nat: {team} is dedans — everything goes to the opposition
wizard.belote.1.title: The goal
wizard.belote.1.body: Belote is played by two fixed teams: you and the player across from you. Each round you get 8 cards from a 32-card pack. One team "takes" trumps and must then score more than the opposition.
wizard.belote.2.title: The jack rules
wizard.belote.2.body: In trumps the jack counts 20 and the nine 14, then ace 11, ten 10, king 4 and queen 3. In the other suits: ace 11, ten 10, king 4, queen 3, jack 2. That is 152 points, plus 10 for the last trick.
wizard.belote.3.title: Trumps are offered
wizard.belote.3.body: Everyone gets 5 cards first; then one card is turned face up. In the first round you may take that suit. If nobody wants it, in the second round you may name a different suit. If still nobody takes, the cards are dealt again.
wizard.belote.4.title: Annonces
wizard.belote.4.body: Combinations in your hand score: three in sequence (tierce) 20, four (cinquante) 50, five (cent) 100, four of a kind 100 — nines 150 and jacks even 200. Only the team with the best combination scores its annonces; the other gets nothing.
wizard.belote.5.title: Belote-rebelote and scoring
wizard.belote.5.body: Holding king and queen of trumps is belote-rebelote: 20 points, and it always counts. At the end the taking team must have more than the opposition; fall short and they are dedans, with everything going to the other side. First team to 501 wins.
guide.belote.title: Belote
guide.belote.summary: The French team game: trumps from a turned card, plus annonces from the hand.
guide.belote.ploegen.title: Fixed teams
guide.belote.ploegen.body: You and the player opposite form one team. You play with 32 cards, eventually 8 each, so eight tricks per round. First team to 501 points wins the match.
guide.belote.waarden.title: The jack rules
guide.belote.waarden.body: The same values as klaverjassen: in trumps the jack counts 20 and the nine 14, then ace 11, ten 10, king 4 and queen 3. In the other suits ace 11, ten 10, king 4, queen 3, jack 2. That is 152 points; the last trick pays 10 more.
guide.belote.bieden.title: Trumps are offered
guide.belote.bieden.body: Here is the big difference with klaverjassen: you do not pick trumps freely. Everyone gets five cards first and then one card is turned face up. In the first round you may take that suit — whoever takes it puts the card in their hand. If nobody wants it, in the second round you may name another suit. If still nobody takes, the cards go back and the next player deals again.
guide.belote.annonces.title: Annonces
guide.belote.annonces.body: Unlike roem in klaverjassen, annonces are about combinations in your hand, not what lands in one trick. Three in sequence in one suit is a tierce (20), four a cinquante (50), five a cent (100). Four of a kind is a carré: 100, but nines 150 and jacks 200. And note: only the team holding the very best combination scores its annonces — the other team gets none at all.
guide.belote.punten.title: Belote-rebelote, dedans and capot
guide.belote.punten.body: King and queen of trumps in one hand is called belote-rebelote and pays 20, separate from the annonces and regardless of who wins the round. At the end each team adds card points, annonces and belote. The taking team must have more than the opposition; fall short and they are dedans, with everything going to the other side. All eight tricks is capot: 100 extra.
tile.hartenjagen: The game where you really do not want the points.
harten.intro: Every player for themselves, 52 cards, no trumps. Each heart costs 1 penalty point and the queen of spades 13 — and before every round you pass three cards on.
harten.passWaiting: Your cards are ready — waiting for the others.
harten.moon: {name} shot the moon! Zero points for {name}, 26 for everyone else.
harten.goal: Aim: as few penalty points as possible. The game ends as soon as somebody reaches {n}.
harten.sessionWon: {name} wins with the lowest score: {points} points.
coach.tip.hjPass: Pass on what will hurt you later: the queen of spades, and the ace or king of spades that would capture her. High hearts can go too.
coach.tip.hjPassNone: No passing this round — you play the hand you were dealt.
coach.tip.hjOpening: The two of clubs always leads. Nobody may discard a penalty card in this first trick.
coach.tip.hjLead: You lead. Hearts are not allowed yet, because none have fallen. Play low and let somebody else take the trick.
coach.tip.hjLeadBroken: Hearts are broken, so you may lead them now. Staying low is still the safest choice.
coach.tip.hjDuck: This trick already holds {points} penalty points. Stay below the highest card and it will not be yours.
coach.tip.hjDiscard: You cannot follow suit: throw away your most dangerous card. The queen of spades first, then high hearts.
wizard.hartenjagen.1.title: Thinking in reverse
wizard.hartenjagen.1.body: In Hearts everybody plays for themselves, and you do not want the tricks. Every heart you collect costs 1 penalty point, the queen of spades costs 13. The first player to reach 100 points ends the game — and the player with the lowest score wins.
wizard.hartenjagen.2.title: The penalty cards
wizard.hartenjagen.2.body: There are exactly 26 penalty points in every deal: thirteen hearts worth 1 point each, plus the queen of spades for 13. Every other card is free. There are no trumps: the highest card of the suit led wins the trick.
wizard.hartenjagen.3.title: Passing three cards
wizard.hartenjagen.3.body: Before every round you set aside three cards for another player: first to the left, then to the right, then across the table, and in the fourth round not at all. You choose before you see what comes back — so pass on whatever will hurt you later.
wizard.hartenjagen.4.title: Leading and following
wizard.hartenjagen.4.body: Whoever holds the two of clubs leads it. Following suit is compulsory; if you cannot follow you may discard freely — except in the first trick, where no penalty card may fall. You may only lead hearts once hearts have fallen somewhere.
wizard.hartenjagen.5.title: Shooting the moon
wizard.hartenjagen.5.body: Collect all 26 penalty points in a single round and the whole thing flips: you score 0 and the other three score 26 each. That is shooting the moon. It is a gamble — miss a single heart and you are the one sitting on 25 points.
guide.hartenjagen.title: Hearts
guide.hartenjagen.summary: Everyone for themselves, no trumps, and points you would rather avoid.
guide.hartenjagen.omgekeerd.title: Avoiding points
guide.hartenjagen.omgekeerd.body: Hearts is the odd one out in this app. There are no teams, there is no bidding and there is no trump suit. You play for yourself, and your goal is to collect as few points as possible. The game runs until somebody has 100 penalty points; at that moment whoever has the lowest total wins.
guide.hartenjagen.strafpunten.title: Hearts and the black lady
guide.hartenjagen.strafpunten.body: The game uses 52 cards, thirteen per player. Every heart that ends up in your tricks costs 1 penalty point, and the queen of spades — the black lady — costs 13. Exactly 26 points per round. Every other card counts for nothing.
guide.hartenjagen.doorgeven.title: Passing three cards
guide.hartenjagen.doorgeven.body: Before the first trick everybody passes three cards on: in the first round to the left, in the second to the right, in the third to the player opposite, and in the fourth round not at all. Then the pattern starts over. Everybody chooses at the same time, so you do not yet know what you will get back.
guide.hartenjagen.spelen.title: Leading, following and breaking hearts
guide.hartenjagen.spelen.body: The player holding the two of clubs leads and must play that card. Following suit is compulsory. In the first trick no penalty card may be discarded, unless you have nothing else. You may only lead hearts once hearts have fallen in an earlier trick — hearts are then broken. The queen of spades, however, may always be led.
guide.hartenjagen.alles.title: Shooting the moon
guide.hartenjagen.alles.body: Whoever collects all 26 penalty points in one round turns the tables: they score 0 and the other three score 26 each. That can turn a hopeless hand into a chance — but it rarely comes off, and a single missed heart costs you almost the full 26.
tile.boerenbridge: Predict exactly how many tricks you will take.
boeren.intro: Every player for themselves, and every round deals a different number of cards. You predict how many tricks you will take — and then you have to take exactly that many.
boeren.turned: Turned card — that suit is trumps
boeren.bidPrompt: How many tricks will you take? Pick a number from 0 to {n}.
boeren.goal: Aim: take exactly what you predicted — one too many costs as much as one too few.
coach.tip.bbBid: Predict how many of the {n} tricks you will take. Zero is allowed — and is often the hardest to deliver.
coach.tip.bbScrew: You are the last to predict, and the total may not add up exactly: one number is therefore blocked.
coach.tip.bbNeed: You still need {n} more trick(s). Take them as cheaply as you can — you will want your high cards later.
coach.tip.bbDone: You have made your prediction. Every further trick now costs you points: stay under the trick.
coach.tip.bbOver: You are already {n} trick(s) over your prediction. The damage is done, but the fewer you still take, the better.
wizard.boerenbridge.1.title: Take exactly what you say
wizard.boerenbridge.1.body: In Oh Hell everybody plays for themselves. Before each round you predict how many tricks you will take. Take exactly that many and you score; take one too many or too few and it costs you points. Overshooting is just as bad as falling short.
wizard.boerenbridge.2.title: A different hand size every round
wizard.boerenbridge.2.body: That is what sets this game apart: the number of cards changes. You start with one card, then two, up to eight — three rounds on eight — and then back down to one. Seventeen rounds in all. With one card in hand predicting is a gamble; with eight it is arithmetic.
wizard.boerenbridge.3.title: The trump card is turned up
wizard.boerenbridge.3.body: After the deal the top card of the stock is turned face up. That suit is trumps for this round. If the stock is empty — because every card has been dealt — the round is played without trumps.
wizard.boerenbridge.4.title: Predicting and playing
wizard.boerenbridge.4.body: The player to the dealer’s left predicts first, the dealer last. That same player then leads. Following suit is compulsory; if you cannot follow you may play anything, trumps included — trumping is never required.
wizard.boerenbridge.5.title: Scoring
wizard.boerenbridge.5.body: Get your prediction right and you score 10 points plus 3 for every trick taken. Three predicted and three taken is therefore 19 points. Get it wrong and you lose 3 points per trick of difference. After the final round the highest total wins.
guide.boerenbridge.title: Oh Hell
guide.boerenbridge.summary: Predict your trick count exactly — and every round deals a different number of cards.
guide.boerenbridge.doel.title: Exactly, not as many as possible
guide.boerenbridge.doel.body: In Oh Hell — known in Dutch as boerenbridge — everybody plays for themselves. Before each round you say how many tricks you think you will take. Take exactly that many and it scores; take more or fewer and it costs you. That makes the game peculiar: taking one trick too many is just as expensive as missing one.
guide.boerenbridge.rondes.title: The hand size changes
guide.boerenbridge.rondes.body: This is the only game in this app where the hand size varies. The championship rules run seventeen rounds: one card, then two, up to eight, then three rounds on eight cards, and back down to one. With one card predicting is nearly a gamble; with eight you can genuinely count. The app also offers two shorter shapes for anyone who does not fancy seventeen rounds.
guide.boerenbridge.voorspellen.title: Predicting
guide.boerenbridge.voorspellen.body: After the deal the next card of the stock is turned face up: that suit is trumps. Everybody then predicts, starting to the dealer’s left; the dealer speaks last. Predicting zero is allowed, and is often the hardest to deliver. Some tables screw the dealer: they may not name the number that would make the total add up exactly to the number of tricks. In this app that rule is off by default.
guide.boerenbridge.spelen.title: Playing
guide.boerenbridge.spelen.body: The player to the dealer’s left leads. Following suit is compulsory. If you cannot follow the suit led you may play anything — trumps included, but trumping is never required. The highest trump wins the trick; without a trump it is the highest card of the suit led.
guide.boerenbridge.punten.title: Scoring
guide.boerenbridge.punten.body: A correct prediction scores 10 points plus 3 per trick taken. Predict three and take three and you get 19. Get it wrong and you lose 3 points per trick of difference, in either direction. A correct zero scores 10, the minimum for anyone who got it right. After the final round the highest total wins.
tile.tarot: 78 cards, trumps and the Fool — for 3, 4 or 5.
tarot.intro: The official Fédération Française de Tarot game: 78 cards with 21 trumps and the Fool, for 3, 4 or 5 players. Rule variants are chosen at the start.
tarot.hint.3: With three everybody gets 24 cards and a dog of six is left over.
tarot.hint.4: The usual form: 18 cards each, a dog of six, and the taker stands alone.
tarot.hint.5: 15 cards each. The taker calls a king and so gains a secret partner.
tarot.chien: The dog — the taker puts back just as many cards
tarot.bidPrompt: What do you bid? The higher the contract, the heavier it counts.
tarot.redeal: Everybody passed — the next dealer deals again.
tarot.callPrompt: Call a suit: the {rank} of that suit becomes your partner.
tarot.ecartPrompt: Put cards aside for your discard ({done}/{total}). No kings and no oudlers.
tarot.petitAuBout: Petit au bout — the 1 of trumps fell on the last trick.
tarot.goal: Target: 56 points with no oudler, 51 with one, 41 with two, 36 with all three.
coach.tip.ttBid: You hold {atouts} trumps. With plenty of trumps, the 21 or the Fool it is worth taking; otherwise pass and let somebody else carry the risk.
coach.tip.ttCall: Call a suit you are strong in but whose king you do not hold — that puts your partner exactly where you need them.
coach.tip.ttEcart: Empty one suit completely, so you can trump it later. Kings and oudlers may not go, trumps only if there is no other way.
coach.tip.ttLead: You lead. As taker you draw trumps to empty the opposition; as a defender you would rather play a suit.
coach.tip.ttMustTrump: You cannot follow the suit, so you must trump — and go higher than what is already down if you can.
coach.tip.ttExcuse: The Fool can always be played: it never wins, but it stays in your own tricks and is worth 4.5 points.
wizard.tarot.1.title: A completely different deck
wizard.tarot.1.body: Tarot uses 78 cards: four suits of fourteen — with a knight between jack and queen — plus 21 trumps and the Fool. You play with three, four or five. One player, the taker, takes on all the others.
wizard.tarot.2.title: The oudlers set your target
wizard.tarot.2.body: Three cards are called oudlers: the 1 of trumps, the 21 and the Fool. Each is worth 4.5 points and together they set the taker’s target: 56 points with none, 51 with one, 41 with two and 36 with all three. The more oudlers, the easier it gets.
wizard.tarot.3.title: Bidding
wizard.tarot.3.body: Everybody speaks once. Petite and guard let you take the dog; with guard without and guard against it stays face down but counts double heavy. The multipliers run from ×1 up through ×2, ×4 and ×6.
wizard.tarot.4.title: The dog and the discard
wizard.tarot.4.body: With petite and guard the dog is turned face up, the taker picks it up and puts back just as many cards — the discard. No kings and no oudlers may go there, and trumps only when there is no other way. Those cards simply count for the taker at the end.
wizard.tarot.5.title: Play, scoring and announcements
wizard.tarot.5.body: Following suit is compulsory; if you cannot follow you must trump, and even go higher than what is down. The Fool may always be played, never wins, and stays in your own tricks. At the end: 25 points plus the difference to your target, times your contract’s multiplier. Before the first trick you can still show a poignée (20/30/40) or announce a slam (400, or −200 if it goes wrong).
guide.tarot.title: French Tarot
guide.tarot.summary: 78 cards, trumps and the Fool — the FFT rulebook, for three, four or five players.
guide.tarot.kaarten.title: Seventy-eight cards
guide.tarot.kaarten.body: Tarot has a deck of its own. Four suits of fourteen cards: ace up to ten, then jack, knight, queen and king — one court card more than you are used to. Alongside them 21 trumps numbered 1 to 21, the 21 being the highest. And one card on its own: the Fool. Seventy-eight in all.
guide.tarot.bouts.title: The oudlers and the card values
guide.tarot.bouts.body: Three cards are called oudlers: the 1 of trumps (the petit), the 21 and the Fool. They are worth 4.5 points, as is every king. A queen counts 3.5, a knight 2.5, a jack 1.5 and every other card 0.5. Ninety-one points in total. More importantly: the more oudlers the taker has in their tricks, the fewer points they need — 56 with none, 51 with one, 41 with two, 36 with all three.
guide.tarot.bieden.title: The four contracts
guide.tarot.bieden.body: Starting to the dealer’s left everybody speaks once, each time higher than what is down. Petite (×1) and guard (×2) let the taker pick up the dog. With guard without (×4) the dog stays face down but still counts for them; with guard against (×6) it goes to the defence. If everybody passes, the cards are dealt again.
guide.tarot.chien.title: The dog, the discard and the called king
guide.tarot.chien.body: With petite and guard the dog goes face up on the table, the taker picks it up and puts back the same number of cards. No kings and no oudlers may go into that discard, and trumps only when there really is no other way. Playing with five, the taker first calls a king: whoever holds that card is their partner — but that stays secret until the card falls. Call a king you hold yourself and you play alone against four.
guide.tarot.spelen.title: Trump, and go higher
guide.tarot.spelen.body: Following suit is compulsory. If you cannot follow the suit led you must play a trump. If a trump is already down you must also go higher when you can; if you cannot, you still have to play a trump. With no trumps at all you discard freely. The Fool stands outside all of this: it may always be played, it never wins, and it stays in your own side’s tricks — unless you play it on the very last trick.
guide.tarot.punten.title: Settling up, and the bonuses
guide.tarot.punten.body: The taker counts their points and compares them with their target. The result is 25 points plus the difference, times their contract’s multiplier. If somebody took the 1 of trumps on the last trick, another 10 is added — also multiplied, and for or against the taker. On top of that come two bonuses that are not multiplied. The poignée: showing enough trumps before your first card is worth 20, 30 or 40 points — and they go to whoever wins the deal, no matter who showed them. And the slam: taking every trick is 200, announced even 400, but an announced slam you fail to make costs 200. What the taker wins, the others pay between them: with four they get three shares, with five two and their partner one.
tarot.options.title: Rule variants
tarot.options.hint: The default is always the Fédération Française de Tarot rulebook. If your table plays it differently, change it here.
tarot.chelemPrompt: Do you announce a slam? Taking every trick pays 400, failing costs 200. You then lead the first trick.
tarot.poigneePrompt: Do you show a poignée? The bonus goes to whoever wins the deal, no matter who showed it.
tarot.poigneeScored: Poignée: {pts} points for whoever won the deal.
tarot.chelemMissed: Slam announced but not made — 200 points off.
coach.tip.ttChelem: Only announce a slam if you expect to take every single trick: 400 points extra, but 200 off if it goes wrong.
coach.tip.ttPoignee: Showing costs you nothing: the bonus goes to whoever wins the deal anyway. It does give away how many trumps you hold.
scorebord.manualHint: Manual: you type the points for each round yourself. Works for any game.
scorebord.autoHint: {game}: mark what happened and the app works out the points — by the same rules as the game itself.
scorebord.hj.check: Careful: {total} points entered, there should be {expected} to share out.
